Session 10 · Module 4 closes · Oct 10, 2026

ITELECT4 | itelect4-backend goes live, itelect4-project calls it

Before we start

  1. Both repos open, and both running. npm run dev in itelect4-backend — it should print API on http://localhost:4000 and MongoDB connected. npm run dev in itelect4-project as well. Nothing needs json-server today — if your Courses page shows an error this morning, that is correct, and Part 4 is where it stops.
  2. Your GT4 Part 1 backend is what today builds on. If it does not run this morning, fix that first — everything from here is added to it.
  3. Sign in to MongoDB . One setting there has to change before anything can reach your database.
  4. Sign in to GitHub, and have both repos pushed and clean. Vercel deploys what is on GitHub, not what is on your disk.
  5. A Vercel account. Sign in with GitHub at vercel.com — the free Hobby plan, no card. Making one is the first two minutes of the deployment block.
  6. Postman. Same as Session 9. Today the same requests get sent at an address that is not your laptop.

Good to know

  • Two deployments today. They depend on each other in a circle: the backend needs the frontend's address for , and the frontend needs the backend's address for its API calls. Neither address exists until that side is deployed. The way out is the order this session uses -- deploy the backend, deploy the frontend, then go back and fix one variable on the backend.

Finished today and submitted today. This is what closes GT4 and Module 4.

Both repos work, and neither knows the other exists

Eight sessions of frontend and two of backend, with no wire between them

  • itelect4-backend runs on your laptop. Seven routes, register and login, a token that guards the five submission routes, and real rows in . Everything you tried it with was Postman.
  • itelect4-project runs on your laptop too. Six routed pages, a cached list, a validated form. GT3 was submitted in Session 8.
  • Its data came from db.json. json-server on port 3001, reading a file committed to the repo -- every row on screen has been in that file since Session 7. It is gone as of last week, so the Courses page has had nothing to read since.
  • And its login is a name in a box. The store writes demo-token-<name> and ProtectedRoute checks it is not null. No password has ever been typed into this app.
  • Today the frontend starts calling the backend, and both go on the internet. db.json becomes GET /api/courses, demo-token-<name> becomes a token /api/auth/login signed, and localhost:4000 becomes a vercel.app address the frontend is told. The seven backend routes are not rewritten today -- they are exactly as Session 9 left them.

Two repos, two deployments, one application by the end of the session.

None of these are new features. They are the six assumptions Session 9 was allowed to make and today is not.

Part 1: the API has no courses, and three pages read them

Three new files on itelect4-backend, holding the first two public routes

  • Session 9 wrote schemas for two of the three interfaces. User and Submission have models, routes and rules. Course was copied across and left alone.
  • Three pages in the frontend read courses. The list, the detail page, and the dropdown in the submission form. All three call json-server today.
  • So the API needs them before anything is rewired. Otherwise switching the frontend over trades one broken half for another.

Courses are read-only reference data, so they need no POST and no token

Three routes exist for submissions. Courses have none.

  • CoursesPage, CourseDetailPage and the submission form all read courses. They call fetchCourses and fetchCourseByCode, which have asked json-server for /courses since Session 7.
  • itelect4-backend has a Course interface and no Course anything else. Session 9 copied all three Session 1 interfaces across and wrote schemas for two of them.
  • So pointing the frontend at the API today would break two pages. The submissions list would work and the course dropdown would be empty, which is the worst of both.
  • Courses are reference data. Nobody creates one through the app, so there is no POST route to write -- one list, one lookup, and a script that puts the three rows in once.
  • And they are public. The course list is what the site shows somebody who has not logged in, so these are the only two routes in the project with no token check in front of them.
  • You need your own three rows back. They were in db.json, which is deleted. git kept it: `git show HEAD:db.json` prints the last committed copy, and an earlier commit in place of HEAD prints an older one. Copy your own values out of it before you write the seed file.

Three new files and eleven lines of route. Then the frontend has everything it needs.

CourseDoc has to be a Pick, because Mongoose will not take an interface

Added under UserDoc and SubmissionDoc, in the file Session 9 wrote

itelect4-backend/src/types/index.tsthe block added below UserDoc and SubmissionDoc

1// Course is the one Session 1 interface with no id field of its own --


2// the code is its identity -- so unlike the two types above there is


3// nothing here to rename and nothing to leave out. Naming all four


4// fields looks like saying nothing, and it is doing one real job:


5// Omit and Pick both produce a MAPPED type, and an interface is not


6// one. The toJSON transform in Course.ts takes Record<string, unknown>;


7// TypeScript hands it a mapped type happily and refuses an interface.


81export type CourseDoc = Pick<


9  Course,


102  "code" | "title" | "units" | "semester"


11>;

19

21  // "a number between 1 and 6", which is what units really is.


224  units: { type: Number, required: true, min: 1, max: 6 },


23

25});

Course has no id to rename, so its toJSON only deletes

Compare it with the same block in User.ts and Submission.ts

itelect4-backend/src/models/Course.tsthe rest of the file

1// User and Submission both rename _id to id here, because the frontend

4// the two fields Mongo added are the only two that have to come out.


5courseSchema.set("toJSON", {


6  transform(_doc, ret: Record<string, unknown>) {


71    delete ret._id;


82    delete ret.__v;


9    return ret;


10  },


11});

13export const Course = model<CourseDoc>("Course", courseSchema);

npm run seed writes the courses once, and running it twice changes nothing

The one script in this project that writes data nobody requested

itelect4-backend/src/seed.tsthe whole file

1import "dotenv/config";


2import mongoose from "mongoose";


3import { connectDB } from "./config/db";


4import { Course } from "./models/Course";


5import { COURSES } from "./data/courses";


6 


7// npm run seed. Run it once after the database is created, and again


8// after anything that empties it. Nothing else in the project writes


9// a course.


10async function seed() {


111  await connectDB();


12 


13  for (const course of COURSES) {


14    // upsert: update the row with this code, or insert it if there is


15    // none. Running this a second time leaves three courses, not six.


162    await Course.updateOne({ code: course.code }, course, { upsert: true });


17  }


18 


19  console.log(`${COURSES.length} courses in ${mongoose.connection.name}`);


20 


21  // Without this the script never ends: the connection is an open


22  // socket, and Node keeps running while one is still open.


233  await mongoose.disconnect();


24}


25 


26seed().catch((err: unknown) => {


27  console.error("Seed failed:", err);


28  process.exit(1);


29});

Try it

  1. GET, in Postman, with no Authorization header at all:
    http://localhost:4000/api/courses
    200, and three courses in this order: CSSWENG, ITELECT3, ITELECT4. No token, and no complaint about one.
  2. GET, lower case in the URL deliberately:
    http://localhost:4000/api/courses/itelect4
    200, and one object, not an array of one, with "code":"ITELECT4" inside it.
  3. GET, a code that is not in the database:
    http://localhost:4000/api/courses/TEST
    404, and { "message": "No course with code \"TEST\"" }. json-server answered 200 and [] for this, which the frontend had to turn into an error itself.
  4. GET, still with no Authorization header:
    http://localhost:4000/api/submissions
    401, "No token. Send Authorization: <token>". Same server, same moment, different answer -- that is the one requireAuth line.

What to notice

Four requests, one of them refused, and the difference between them is which they landed in. That is the whole of public versus private in this project.

Good to know

  • Two routes nothing can reach yet. A router does nothing until something mounts it, and the line that does -- app.use("/api/courses", courseRouter) -- sits in app.ts beside the other two, on the Waiting for the database page. Until it is there, /api/courses answers the 404 that app.ts writes for a URL that does not exist.

Part 2: the routes do not change, but everything around them does

Three code changes, two Atlas clicks, one Vercel project

  • Nothing about the routes changes. The seven you wrote last week and the two you wrote an hour ago are exactly as they are.
  • What changes is everything around them. No startup step, no file, no fixed IP address, and a browser that will start caring where requests come from.
  • Vercel runs the whole app as one function. It starts a copy when a request arrives and stops it when the traffic does. Between two requests, nothing of yours is necessarily still running.

Vercel needs one default export, and this repo has no vercel.json

13app.use(


14  (err: Error, _req: Request, res: Response, _next: NextFunction) => {


15    if (err instanceof mongoose.Error.ValidationError) {

18        errors: Object.values(err.errors).map((e) => e.message),

25      res.status(400).json({


26        message: `"${err.value}" is not a valid id`,


27      });


28      return;


29    }


30 


311    console.error(err);

33  },


34);

Good to know

  • There is no vercel.json in this repo and there does not need to be. Vercel looks for an Express app in app, index or server, at the project root or inside src, with any of the JavaScript or TypeScript extensions -- src/app.ts is on that list, and a default export is all it wants from it.

Keeping the promise makes many requests share one connection

The rest of db.ts: two changes that let it be called from anywhere

itelect4-backend/src/config/db.tsthe rest of the file

1// The promise, kept. Not the connection -- the promise of one. The


2// first caller starts the connect; every caller after it gets this


3// same promise back and waits on the connection already being made.


41let connection: Promise<typeof mongoose> | null = null;


5 


6export function connectDB(): Promise<typeof mongoose> {


7  const uri = process.env.MONGODB_URI;


8 


9  // Fail here, with a sentence, rather than three screens later with a


10  // connection timeout that does not mention .env at all.


11  if (!uri) {


12    throw new Error(


13      "MONGODB_URI is missing. Copy .env.example to .env and fill it in.",


14    );


15  }


16 


172  if (connection === null) {


18    // Without this option, a wrong or unreachable connection string


19    // does not fail -- it sits there for 31 seconds looking like a


20    // hung terminal, and then errors. Five seconds is long enough for


21    // a real Atlas connection and short enough to tell you something


22    // is wrong.


23    connection = mongoose


243      .connect(uri, { serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000 })


25      .then((m) => {


26        console.log("MongoDB connected:", m.connection.name);


27        return m;


28      })


29      .catch((err: unknown) => {


30        // A failed attempt must not be the thing that gets kept. Leave


31        // the rejected promise in place and every request from now on


32        // fails with this same five-second-old error, including the


33        // ones sent after the database comes back.


344        connection = null;


35        throw err;


36      });


37  }


38 


39  return connection;


40}

Click any numbered line.

Good to know

  • Free Atlas clusters allow 500 connections. One connection per request, on a function that can be running in several copies at once, is how a project that worked all semester falls over the day it has users. Holding the promise is a two-line answer to that.

Only the first call starts a connect; the rest await the same promise

connectDB(), traced twice

1

connectDB() is called

From the in app.ts, in front of every request.

Also once from server.ts, when you run it locally.

→
2

if (connection === null)

The question is whether an attempt has STARTED,

not whether the database is open yet.

→
3

return connection

A promise either way, and the caller awaits it.

Nothing in this function waits for the database itself.

FIRST CALL

  • connection is null, so the if runs
  • mongoose.connect() starts the real connection
  • the promise it hands back is stored in connection
  • that promise is returned, and the caller awaits it

EVERY CALL AFTER

  • connection already holds that promise
  • the if is skipped, so nothing new is started
  • the same promise comes back
  • every caller ends up awaiting the one connect

The database is contacted once per instance. Every request after the first awaits a promise that has already resolved, which costs nothing -- and if that one connect fails, the catch puts connection back to null so the next request starts a fresh one.

Atlas has to allow 0.0.0.0/0, because Vercel's addresses change

The Session 9 entry is your own address, and a deployment is not at your address

Only the three environment variables need thought; the rest is clicking through Vercel

Eleven screens, start to finish, ending at /api/health answering db true

  1. Sign in at vercel.com with GitHub, then Add New, then Project.Push to main first. Vercel deploys what is in the repo, not what is on your disk, and an uncommitted file is the most common reason a behaves differently from your laptop. The free Hobby plan is enough and asks for no card.
  2. Choose GitHub as the provider.GitLab, Bitbucket and a dragged-in folder are offered too. Only the Git ones redeploy when you push, which is what GT4 is marked on.
  3. Press Install to let Vercel see your repositories.Vercel cannot list a single repo until this is done, which is why the panel is empty. This screen appears once per GitHub account, so you will not see it again.
  4. On GitHub, choose which repositories Vercel may read, then Install.All repositories is what the screenshot uses and is the least trouble. Only select repositories works as well -- tick itelect4-backend and itelect4-project -- but you have to come back to this page every time you add a repo.
  5. If GitHub asks who you are, press Verify via email.This is GitHub asking, not Vercel. It appears when you have not re-entered your password for a few hours, and installing an app counts as something worth asking about.
  6. Type the code GitHub emailed you and press Verify.It arrives at your DLSL address within a minute; look in spam if it does not. The code in this screenshot is blurred because it works once and is already spent.
  7. Back on Vercel, press Import beside itelect4-backend.The list is every repository Vercel can now see. Import the backend first: the frontend needs the backend's address later today, and the backend does not need the frontend's yet.
  8. Leave Root Directory as ./ , check the preset says Express, then open Environment Variables.Vercel read package.json, found express and chose the preset itself. There is no vercel.json in this repo and none is needed -- src/app.ts with a default export is on the list of places Vercel looks.
  9. Add MONGODB_URI, JWT_SECRET and CORS_ORIGIN, then press Create Project.The first two are the values already in your . CORS_ORIGIN cannot be right yet, because the frontend has no address until later today -- put http://localhost:5173 in it and come back. Production and Preview is the right scope; Development only matters if you run vercel dev. Do not add PORT: on Vercel the default export is the entry point and app.listen never runs.
  10. Press Deploy, and do not press Add beside MongoDB .That integration provisions a new Atlas through Vercel. Yours already exists and its address is in MONGODB_URI. The build takes about a minute.
  11. The preview says No route for GET / . Press Continue to Project.Nothing is wrong. There is no page at / because this repo is an API and not a website, and that 404 is the one your own app.ts writes -- which is how you know Vercel found the default export and the app is running.
  12. Copy the address under Domains and open it with /api/health on the end.It has to answer ok true and db true. ok means the app is running; db means it reached Atlas. If db is false, the IP access list or MONGODB_URI is wrong, and nothing else today will work.

Eight requests prove the live API before the frontend touches it

Eight requests in Postman, at your own deployment's address. Do these before touching the frontend.

Part 3: the browser can hide a reply that arrived perfectly

The one thing that works in Postman and fails in the browser

  • stops a page at one from reading a reply from another, unless that reply says it is allowed to. The browser is what checks for that permission, not the server.
  • Which is why Postman has never needed any of this. Postman is not a browser and has no page, so there is no origin to check and no policy to apply.
  • And why the request still goes. The server runs the route and answers normally. What the browser withholds is the reply, after the work is done.

Postman never needed CORS, because Postman has no origin

The difference is one header on the way out, and who checks for one on the way back

Postman Chrome, Edge or Firefox
The Origin header on the requestNot sent. Postman has no page, so there is no to declare.Origin: https://itelect4-project-xxxx.vercel.app, put there by the browser. Your code can neither set it nor remove it.
Who reads Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the replyNobody. Postman shows the reply whatever headers came with it.The browser, before your code is handed anything.
When that header is missing or holds a different addressNothing changes: 201 and the JSON body, the same as always.fetch() rejects. The reply is thrown away and your .then() never runs.
What is on your screen in that caseThe response body in the lower pane, and a green 201.A red message in the console naming both addresses, then TypeError: Failed to fetch.
What the API did either wayRan the route and saved the row.Ran the route and saved the row. The Network tab shows 201 with the body in it.

This is why a POST can fail in the browser and still have saved the row. The browser hid the reply from your code after the server had already done the work.

Good to know

A CORS error names both addresses, and the request still succeeded

Three of the six are in the error message itself

Part 4: six files change, and db.json leaves the repo

src/api/client.ts does most of it; RegisterPage and authSchema are new

  • src/api/client.ts is where most of it happens. Every call the app makes is already in that one file, which is why Session 7 put them there.
  • The store stops inventing a token and starts being given one. Its shape changes; nothing that reads it does.
  • The login form grows a password, and a register page appears. Until today nobody has ever had an account.
  • db.json and json-server leave the repo. The three courses are in now and the submissions belong to accounts, so the file that has been this app's data since Session 7 has nothing left to serve.

One request() holds the host, the token and the API's own messages

Four copies of the same four lines become one

itelect4-project/src/api/client.tsthe helper every call goes through

1// Every call goes through here: the host, the JSON header, the token


2// when there is one, and the API's own message when it refuses.


31async function request<T>(


42  path: string,


53  init: RequestInit = {},


6): Promise<T> {


7  // getState(), not the useAuthStore hook -- this is not a component,


8  // and it does not need to re-render when the token changes. It only


9  // needs whatever the token is at the moment of the call.


104  const token = useAuthStore.getState().token;


11 


12  const res = await fetch(`${API_URL}${path}`, {


13    ...init,


14    headers: {


15      "Content-Type": "application/json",


16      // The exact header requireAuth reads: the word Bearer, one


17      // space, then the token. No token in the store means no header


18      // at all, which is what the public course routes want.


195      ...(token ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : {}),


20      ...init.headers,


21    },


22  });


23 


24  if (!res.ok) {


25    // Every refusal this API sends has a message field. Reading it is


26    // the difference between "Could not save the submission" and


27    // "repoUrl must start with https://github.com/".


286    const body = await res.json().catch(() => null);


29    throw new Error(body?.message ?? `Request failed (${res.status})`);


30  }


31 


327  return res.json();


33}


34 

Click any numbered line.

Good to know

  • Four functions used to repeat the same four lines with a different invented message. Now there is one place that knows the host, one place that attaches the token, and one place that reads the API's own sentence out of a failed reply -- and adding the AI endpoint next session is one more call to it.

Good to know

  • An import loop is not a style question -- it breaks at runtime, unpredictably, depending on which module the bundler evaluates first. Keeping the fetching in the pages and the state in the store is what makes the arrow point one way.

setSession keeps state only, so the store never imports client.ts

The rest of authStore.ts

itelect4-project/src/store/authStore.tsthe rest of the file

1import { create } from "zustand";


2import { persist } from "zustand/middleware";


3 


4interface AuthState {


5  token:    string | null;


6  userName: string | null;


7  // Two values in, nothing invented. The login page gets them from


8  // the API and hands them here.


91  setSession: (token: string, userName: string) => void;


10  logout:     () => void;


11}


12 


132// This file deliberately does not import ../api/client. client.ts


14// reads the token out of this store on every request, so a store that


15// called client.ts back would be an import loop. Keeping the fetching


16// in the pages and the state here means the arrow only points one way.


173const useAuthStore = create<AuthState>()(


184  persist(


195    (set) => ({


20      token: null,


21      userName: null,


226      setSession: (token, userName) => set({ token, userName }),


23      logout: () => set({ token: null, userName: null }),


24    }),


25    {


267      name: "itelect4-auth",       // the localStorage key it writes to


278      partialize: (state) => ({    // save ONLY these two fields


28        token: state.token,


29        userName: state.userName,


30      }),


31    }


32  )


33);


34 


35export default useAuthStore;


36 


37// The token is good for two hours -- that is the expiresIn in


38// itelect4-backend's login route. Persist keeps it across a reload,


39// so the app can come back holding one the API has already stopped


40// accepting: the next request answers 401, and Log out then log in


41// again is the fix.

Click any numbered line.

Good to know

  • Anything in localStorage can be read by any JavaScript running on the page, so a cross-site scripting hole would expose this token. The answer used in production is a cookie marked HttpOnly, which the browser refuses to hand to JavaScript at all -- that needs cookie handling in Express and a credentials setting on both sides of , which is more than today has room for. localStorage is the right trade for this project; knowing that it is a trade is the part worth keeping.

92export const loginSchema = z.object({

247  name: z.string().min(1, "Your name is required."),


25});

The frontend deploys, then the backend needs one more edit and a redeploy

The last two screens are the backend's settings, not this project's

  1. At vercel.com: Add New, then Project.Have the backend's address ready before you start, because the VITE_API_URL box asks for it. It is the Domains line on the backend project's page, and it reads https://itelect4-backend-xxxx.vercel.app.
  2. Press Import beside itelect4-project.Vercel finds vite in package.json and picks the Vite preset by itself: Build Command npm run build, Output Directory . Both are already right, so change neither. This is a different preset from the backend's, read from a different package.json.
  3. Add one variable, VITE_API_URL, then press Deploy.Key VITE_API_URL, value your backend's address, with no trailing slash and no /api on the end, because client.ts adds the paths. Production and Preview, the same as the backend. Vite bakes this into the bundle while it builds, so changing it later means another before it means anything.
  4. Press Continue to Project, then open /courses on the new address.The preview on this screen is your own app. Open https://itelect4-project-xxxx.vercel.app/courses: the three courses load, which on its own proves the browser reached your API, because those rows exist only in .
  5. Now open the BACKEND project and paste the frontend's address into CORS_ORIGIN.Check the project name at the top before you type: this is itelect4-backend, not the one you just deployed. Environment Variables in the left sidebar, the CORS_ORIGIN row, then the Value box -- replace http://localhost:5173 with https://itelect4-project-xxxx.vercel.app, no trailing slash. This is the edit everyone forgets, because the backend was working ten minutes ago and nothing about it has changed.
  6. Press Save, then Redeploy, with Production chosen.Save stores the new value and changes nothing that is already running, because an is read when the app starts. The redeploy is what makes it real. When it finishes, open https://itelect4-project-xxxx.vercel.app/register and make an account: you land on /submissions, and the whole circle is closed.

Click the picture to see it full screen

Good to know

  • This is the circle from the first page closing. The backend needed the frontend's address and the frontend needed the backend's, and neither address existed until that side was deployed. Deploying the backend first with a placeholder in CORS_ORIGIN, then coming back to correct it, is the way out.

Nine routes now, and only the five submission routes need a token

Seven from Session 9, two added today

Method and path Token? Answers
GET /api/healthNo{ ok: true, db: true } once is connected
GET /api/coursesNoEvery course, sorted by code
GET /api/courses/:codeNoOne course, or 404
POST /api/auth/registerNo201 and the new user, or 409
POST /api/auth/loginNo200 and a token, or 401
GET /api/submissionsYesOnly this token's rows, newest first
GET /api/submissions/:idYesOne row, or 404 if it is not yours
POST /api/submissionsYes201 and the row, with an id and an owner
PATCH /api/submissions/:idYes200 and the row after the change
DELETE /api/submissions/:idYes204, and nothing in the body

The two public ones are public because a visitor who has not logged in still sees the course list. Everything under /api/submissions belongs to somebody.

Six symptoms, and not one of them names its own cause

Read the left column first; the right one is what is really wrong

What you see

  • A blank white page, and a bundle about half its usual size: 257 kB against 467 kB.
  • Every request answers 500, and the log says MONGODB_URI is missing.
  • The browser console says the reply has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, but the row WAS created.
  • It works locally and every request times out at .
  • You changed an in Vercel and nothing changed.
  • Everything works, then two hours later every list is empty and every save answers 401.

What is actually wrong

  • VITE_API_URL was not set when the frontend was built. client.ts throws at import, so the bundler dropped everything after it.
  • The variables were added to Vercel's Preview environment and this is Production, or they were added after the last deploy.
  • CORS_ORIGIN on the backend does not list the frontend's address. The browser blocked the reply, not the request.
  • Atlas still allows only your own IP. Vercel's addresses change, so the entry matches nothing -- it needs 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Nothing reads it until the next deploy. Redeploy, and for the frontend rebuild too, because Vite bakes it in.
  • The token expired. expiresIn is 2h in the login route, and persist kept the dead one across the reload. Log out, log in.

Module 5 is one session, so it starts with the key already made

One session for the whole of Gemini, so the setup happens beforehand

  • The key never goes in git. It is an on the backend, exactly like JWT_SECRET, and it goes in .env.example with no value.
